# How much resin do I need?

> Calculate rectangular or cylindrical mold volume in US fluid ounces or milliliters, subtract embedded object displacement, add cup-loss allowance, and optionally split volume-ratio Parts A and B.

## Calculator
- [Open the calculator](https://metricotter.com/): US tray: a 6 × 4 × 1 in mold (13.3 fl oz) with 10% allowance needs 14.6 fl oz (432.6 mL)—7.3 fl oz each for a 1:1 volume ratio. Metric: a 10 × 5 × 2 cm rectangular mold with 10% cup allowance needs 110.0 mL of mixed resin.

## Guide
- [How to work out how much resin you need](https://metricotter.com/guide/): step-by-step measuring, common mistakes, and ordering checklist.

## Formula and method
Rectangle volume = L × W × depth; Cylinder volume = π × (diameter / 2)² × depth; Mixed batch = (mold volume − displacement) × mold count × (1 + extra / 100).

Compute cavity volume in cubic centimeters (1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 US fl oz = 29.5735 mL). Subtract the volume displaced by embedded wood or inclusions, multiply by the number of molds, and apply your mixing-cup allowance. When your resin specifies a mixing ratio by volume (A:B), divide the total in those exact proportions.

## Limits
Only use the A:B component split when the manufacturer specifies a ratio by volume—never apply a volume split to a resin mixed by weight, because resin and hardener densities differ. Respect each resin maximum single-pour thickness to avoid overheating, bubbling, or cracking.

## Common epoxy types, pour-depth limits, and volume conversions

Always verify mix basis (by volume vs by weight) and maximum single-layer pour thickness on the container datasheet.

| Resin category | Typical mix ratio | Typical max pour depth | Quick volume conversions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Art / tabletop coating epoxy | 1:1 by volume | 1/8 – 1/4 in (3–6 mm) | 1 US fl oz = 29.57 mL |
| Craft / jewelry casting resin | 1:1 or 2:1 by volume | 1/4 – 1/2 in (6–12 mm) | 1 cubic inch = 16.39 mL (0.554 fl oz) |
| Deep-pour river-table epoxy | 2:1 or 3:1 (check volume vs weight) | 1 – 2 in (25–50 mm) | 1 US cup = 8 fl oz = 236.6 mL |
| Laminating / marine epoxy | 2:1 to 5:1 (often by weight/pump) | Thin coats / fiberglass cloth | 1 US quart = 32 fl oz = 946.4 mL |

## Step by step
1. Select rectangle or cylinder and measure the inside cavity dimensions plus the exact fill depth you intend to pour.
2. If embedding wood, stones, or dried items, estimate their displaced volume so you do not overfill the mold.
3. Add a 5% to 15% allowance for resin that clings to mixing cups and stir sticks, especially on small batches.
4. Only check the volume-ratio split if your resin instructions specify mixing by volume (e.g., 1:1 or 2:1 by volume). For weight ratios, weigh each part on a gram scale instead.

## Common mistakes
- Using a volume calculator to split a resin whose product sheet specifies a ratio by weight—Part A and Part B usually have different densities.
- Exceeding the product maximum pour depth per layer. Pouring tabletop epoxy thicker than ~1/4 in (6 mm) can overheat, yellow, bubble, or crack.
- Forgetting cup loss on tiny pours like jewelry or coasters, where 5 to 10 mL stays coated on the mixing cup walls.
- Guessing cure math when a mold has tapered sides or rounded corners—measure average width or test capacity with water first (dry completely before pouring).

## Worked examples
### Example 1
Metric: a 10 × 5 × 2 cm rectangular mold with 10% cup allowance needs 110.0 mL of mixed resin.

### Example 2
US tray: a 6 × 4 × 1 in mold (13.3 fl oz) with 10% allowance needs 14.6 fl oz (432.6 mL)—7.3 fl oz each for a 1:1 volume ratio.

### Example 3
Round mold: a 10 cm diameter cylinder filled 2 cm deep holds about 157.1 mL (5.3 fl oz) before allowance.
